analysis.one_liner: Requires large websites and apps to get your express permission before collecting or selling your personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote: Senator Rick Scott introduced it alone, with zero cosponsors, and the Senate Commerce Committee took no action on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DATA Act would have forced large websites, apps, social networks, search engines, and phone operating systems — those with at least 30 million U.S. users that use algorithms to rank or promote content — to get your express permission before collecting personal data like your habits, beliefs, preferences, or location, and before selling or sharing that data with anyone else. You could have withdrawn consent and demanded deletion of your data at any time, and platforms would have had to tell you, in plain language, exactly what data they collect and the names and countries of any companies they share it with. The Federal Trade Commission could have enforced the rules, and individual users could have sued violators for at least $5,000.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of Americans who use large websites, social networks, search engines, and mobile apps. Their personal data — habits, traits, preferences, beliefs, and location — could no longer be collected without express opt-in consent, could not be sold or shared with third parties without permission, could be deleted on request, and they would be told in plain language which companies receive it and where those companies are based [S3]. Anyone harmed could sue for at least $5,000 plus attorney's fees [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of large websites and apps

how_it_helps.text: Blocks platforms with 30 million or more U.S. monthly users that use content-ranking algorithms from collecting personal data about a person's habits, traits, preferences, beliefs, or location without that person's express consent, and lets users revoke consent and demand deletion of their data at any time.

Stops those platforms from selling, sharing, or conveying a user's data to third parties without express consent, and requires notices naming the specific data shared, each third-party recipient, and that recipient's country of origin.

Gives the Federal Trade Commission enforcement power over violations and creates a private right of action so any individual can sue in state or federal court, with a guaranteed minimum recovery of $5,000 plus attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs.

Requires the consent notice to be written in plain language, shown separately from the terms of service, and re-presented at every login and whenever terms change, so permission is informed rather than buried in fine print.

analysis.who_pays: Large internet platforms and the digital advertising and data-brokerage businesses built on their data. They would lose the default ability to harvest and monetize user data without affirmative permission, and would bear compliance costs for consent systems, notices, and deletion requests [S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to users through more ads or paywalls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires a consent notice at every login unless the user waives it, which could produce constant pop-up fatigue and train people to click through without reading — the same problem that made European cookie banners easy to ignore.

The private right of action sets a guaranteed floor of $5,000 per plaintiff and declares any violation a 'concrete and particularized injury,' which could invite high-volume lawsuits over technical notice mistakes even when no user suffered actual harm.
The 30-million-user threshold exempts smaller websites and apps entirely, so mid-size sites could keep collecting and selling the same kinds of data with no consent requirement at all.

Requiring express opt-in consent before any data collection could make free, ad-supported services harder to run, and platforms might respond by charging fees or degrading features — costs that would land on ordinary users.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: ordinary users of the biggest platforms would regain control over data that today is collected and monetized by default, with teeth in the form of FTC enforcement and a $5,000-minimum private lawsuit [S3]. The costs are mostly design flaws rather than reasons to reject the idea — notice fatigue from per-login prompts, litigation risk from a generous private right of action, and a size threshold that leaves smaller sites unregulated. A better-drafted bill could fix all three, but no such revision ever happened because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and sat there untouched until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott of Florida introduced the DATA Act in the Senate on March 7, 2023. No other senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which has jurisdiction over internet and communications policy. That was the final action of any kind.
The committee never held a markup, never reported the bill to the floor, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large internet platforms and the data brokers and advertisers who buy their user data are better off: nothing changed, so they continue collecting and monetizing personal data without express user consent.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DATA Act, which would require large algorithm-driven platforms to obtain express user consent before collecting or selling personal data.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Senate committee of jurisdiction over internet policy
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 7, 2023 and took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor consideration — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: The other 99 sitting senators
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party cosponsored the bill, and no senator moved it out of committee or asked for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted enough support to reveal a partisan split: a single Republican sponsored it, no Democrat or Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Large internet platforms (social networks, search engines, video sharing, mobile operating systems)
industries.note: These companies' business models rest on collecting behavioral data by default and using algorithms to rank content; the bill would have made express opt-in consent, deletion rights, and detailed disclosures mandatory, directly constraining how they monetize users. Because the bill died, nothing changed for them.

Ad networks are explicitly covered platforms under the bill's definitions, and restrictions on selling or sharing personal data would have cut off the data flows that fuel targeted advertising. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against users' control over their own data.

industries.industry: Data brokers and third-party data recipients
industries.note: The bill would have required platforms to name every third party receiving user data and its country of origin, and to obtain consent before any conveyance — exposing and constraining an industry that mostly operates without consumers' knowledge.
